Question: Why did World of Warcraft become so popular in the first place?
Because it was the first mmo of its kind at that scale. And by the standards of the time, was pretty good.
Wait a second. Everquest was out years before WoW.

And WoW was waaaaaay more accessible than it, DAoC, FFXI, etc. For starters, death only resulted in a ghostly corpse run and a relatively minor equipment repair bill. In MMOs before it, a death meant you'd lose hours worth of grinded XP (and worse, risk losing your equipment if your corpse wasn't near trustworthy allies). Furthermore, WoW had a ton of soloable content in the form of quests, whereas most previously released MMOs required a party just to XP grind (CoH was an exception to this, but it too had the XP issues). And I do mean grind.

So yeah, WoW introduced us to questing as a means to level, which was much more varied than grinding in a group. So you were able to quest while trying to get a dungeon group together, a dungeon which was instanced I might add, so you don't compete with other groups for spawns and drops (which could cause problems). In FFXI, I'd spend an hour+ fishing before finding a group to grind mobs with, and then hope we'd go at it for over an hour, or I wouldn't even recoup the cost it took to pay for a chocobo ride to our farming spot. And if I died during the grind, well, there goes all the progress I'd made over the last hour of grinding (and this game was much more forgiving than EQ in that regard).

WoW made it so you could play an MMO casually without needing to marry yourself to a guild. So by first of it's kind he doesn't mean first MMO, but "first MMO that was designed to be accessible to a wide audience"

Around the mid 30s up to he early 40s it was more efficient to grind mobs (Sardor Isle was a common place grind levels). Leveling up in vanilla wow had a lot of XP issues, not nearly as bad as most other MMO's but it wasn't addressed until the XP squish around patch 2.3 which simply lowered the per level requirements.

I'd argue that WoW leveling wasn't fixed until Cata came out and the entire leveling up experience was reworked to match the quest content you were going though.

Yeah, content was a bit thinner by today's standards, but they swept the competition of the time. They've gotten even better at it since then, but if you're evaluating how much Vanilla WoW changed the genre, you need to compare it to things that were out at the same time, not the game after years of polish, or to games which were inspired by it. We're talking about what made it popular initially after all.

This is very well-informed explanation. Anyone who survived UO, EQ, DAoC, FFXI, SWG, Lineage, etc., etc., etc. can vouch for this. The laundry list of even simple game mechanics that were made convenient and user friendly in WoW is pretty damn extensive when you compare it to all MM forerunners and early contemporaries.

Psychology: If you always give a negative reward to someone for something they did they lose interest, if you always give them a positive reward happens the same.

But, if you add a random element the brain creates a dependency where the action receives a positive reward sometimes, creating expectation about the result of a task. In other words, it creates an addiction.

It is not the only game that does that, it is also the base for things like gambling. So WoW is pretty much a digital addiction that knew how to milk this theory in better ways than the competition.
